
# Methods {#sec-appendix-methods}

This appendix provides more details on how we measure interbranch representation, our data collection process, and the methods with which we analyze the data.  

## The data generating process 

The data we received in response to our Freedom of Information Act requests include several filtering processes, leading to an under-count of true levels of interbranch representation. First, the agency had to make a record of the interaction. If a staffer from a congressional office talked to someone they know at an agency over the phone, they may not always make a record of it. However, they often do, because internal agency procedures often have precise guidance about recording interactions with members of congress, <!--cite proceedures manual-->  which often include minimum response times and signature levels. Nearly all agencies use a correspondence tracking system provided by a government contractor that standardizes information and tracks cases that need followup. Members of congress are generally tagged as "VIP" or "Priority" in these tracking systems. <!---We observed this in the data we received and it was confirmed in interview with former officials. Anything having to do with congress will be treated differently. Anything going out always goes way up the chain. For executive regulatory agencies (rather than the independent agencies) this means that every agency potentially involved as well as the White House sign off on anything sent to a member of Congress. ## Coding Types of Interbranch Representation

This section goes into more detail on how we coded types of interbranch representation. 

To account for uncertainty or ambiguity in our coding, we also identified the level of certainty of each decision made during the hand-coding process (1 = very certain, 2 = fairly certain, and 3 = toss-up), as well as the next best guess for an alternative type.
